prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

candidates.label: Activation Functions
candidates.description: Non-linear functions applied to neuron outputs that introduce non-linearity into the network, enabling it to learn complex patterns; common examples include sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and softmax.
coverage_criteria: List at least three activation functions and their typical output ranges.
Explain why non-linear activation functions are necessary in hidden layers.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Multiple sections list activation functions: the TensorFlow section enumerates relu, sigmoid, tanh, softmax, etc.; the Keras examples use relu and sigmoid.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Activation functions are a building block; this candidate covers their purpose and common types, checkable through identification and selection.

candidates.label: Activation Functions
candidates.description: Activation functions g(z) introduce non-linearity: sigmoid: 1/(1+e^{-z}); tanh: (e^z - e^{-z})/(e^z + e^{-z}); ReLU: max(0,z); leaky ReLU: max(εz,0).
coverage_criteria: The student can list at least three common activation functions, provide their formulas, and describe when each might be used.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly lists the formulas for sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and leaky ReLU under the 'Activation Functions' heading.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a focused check on a small set of functions that are critical for neural network non-linearity.

candidates.label: Sigmoid Activation Function
candidates.description: The sigmoid function f(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z}) maps any real-valued number to a value between 0 and 1, used as an activation function in neural network neurons to introduce non-linearity.
coverage_criteria: Compute the sigmoid of a given number.
Explain why non-linearity is important in neural networks.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The article introduces the sigmoid function as the activation for each neuron and provides its implementation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific function that can be checked with a simple calculation and a brief explanation.

candidates.label: Função de Ativação Sigmoide
candidates.description: A função sigmoide é uma função de ativação suave e contínua usada em neurônios de redes neurais para permitir o treinamento com gradiente, diferentemente da função degrau.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve definir a função sigmoide e explicar por que ela é preferível à função degrau para treinamento.
O estudante deve saber que a sigmoide é contínua e diferenciável, facilitando o backpropagation.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O texto introduz a função sigmoide como alternativa suave à step_function, justificando seu uso para cálculos de gradiente no treinamento.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Conceito específico de função de ativação, pequeno o suficiente para ser verificado com perguntas sobre sua fórmula e propósito.

candidates.label: Função de Ativação Degrau
candidates.description: Função que transforma o somatório ponderado em uma saída binária: retorna 1 se u >= 0 e -1 caso contrário, usada para classificação binária.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve implementar a função sinal(u) e prever sua saída para diferentes valores de u.
O aluno deve explicar por que a função degrau é adequada para perceptrons simples, mas limitada para problemas não-lineares.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: A função é explicitamente definida no código (`def sinal(u): return 1 if u >= 0 else -1`) e explicada como a etapa final do perceptron para decidir a classe (07:04-07:19).
rationale.granularity_rationale: Trata-se de um componente bem isolado do modelo, podendo ser ensinado e testado separadamente.

candidates.label: Loss Functions for Neural Networks
candidates.description: Loss functions quantify the error between predictions and true values during training; regression uses mean squared error, binary classification uses binary cross-entropy, and multi-class uses categorical cross-entropy.
coverage_criteria: Match loss functions (MSE, binary crossentropy, categorical crossentropy) to problem types.
Explain why cross-entropy is preferred over MSE for classification.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The Keras cheat sheet explicitly mentions loss functions like 'binary_crossentropy', 'categorical_crossentropy', and the ADALINE section discusses mean square error as a quadratic function.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Selecting the right loss is crucial; this candidate covers the main loss types with their usage contexts.

candidates.label: Cost Function (Logistic Loss)
candidates.description: The cost function quantifies the error of the neural network's predictions. The logistic loss (cross-entropy) is commonly used for binary classification, computing the negative average of the log-likelihood.
coverage_criteria: Write the logistic loss formula.
Explain why minimizing the cost function improves the model.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The article introduces the cost function as a measure of how far predictions are from truth, and provides a Python implementation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Knowing the cost function is crucial for understanding training, and it can be checked with a formula recall and explanation.

candidates.label: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
candidates.description: A deep learning architecture designed for grid-structured data, using convolutional layers to automatically learn spatial hierarchies of features, followed by pooling and fully-connected layers.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operations of a convolutional layer (kernel, stride, feature map).
Explain the role of pooling layers in reducing dimensionality.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The Keras cheat sheet provides a complete CNN example with Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Flatten, and Dense layers, and the chart includes Deep Convolutional Network.
rationale.granularity_rationale: CNNs are a cornerstone of modern vision systems; this candidate covers the essential layers and their functions.

anchors: Keras CNN example: Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Flatten

candidates.label: Convolutional Layer Output Size
candidates.description: For a convolutional layer, with input volume size W, filter size F, padding P, the number of output neurons N satisfies a relationship (though the formula is given via normalization example).
coverage_criteria: The student can state that the output size depends on input size, filter size, and padding, and can compute N for simple cases.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions the convolutional layer requirement with a formula involving W, F, P, and N, though the exact formula is obscured by a normalization equation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Understanding how output dimensions relate to layer parameters is a key practical concept for CNNs.

candidates.label: Deep Residual Network (DRN)
candidates.description: An advanced neural network that incorporates skip connections (residual blocks) to allow gradients to flow through very deep architectures, enabling training of networks with hundreds of layers.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is and why it helps training deep networks.
Mention a popular implementation of residual networks (e.g., ResNet).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The chart lists Deep Residual Network as a distinct type, indicating its significance in the taxonomy of neural networks.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Residual connections are a pivotal innovation; this candidate introduces the concept at a checkable level.

candidates.label: TensorFlow and Keras for Neural Networks
candidates.description: Popular open-source Python libraries that provide high-level APIs for constructing, training, and evaluating neural network models, with TensorFlow as the backend and Keras as a simplified interface.
coverage_criteria: Write the code to define a simple neural network using Keras Sequential model.
Explain the difference between TensorFlow and Keras.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source includes dedicated cheat sheets for TensorFlow and Keras with code examples for building models, compiling, and fitting.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Familiarity with these tools is practical; this candidate covers their basic usage as demonstrated.

candidates.label: Keras for deep learning
candidates.description: Keras is a high-level open-source Python library for defining and training neural network models, built on top of TensorFlow.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that Keras simplifies neural network development and is part of the TensorFlow ecosystem.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces Keras as a powerful and easy-to-use free open source Python library for developing and evaluating deep learning models.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept that underpins the entire tutorial; it can be checked with a single explanation.

candidates.label: Sequential model in Keras
candidates.description: A Sequential model allows stacking layers linearly to define a neural network architecture in Keras.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a Sequential model object and add layers one by one using model.add().

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source states 'Models in Keras are defined as a sequence of layers. We create a Sequential model and add layers one at a time.' and provides code.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a key architectural pattern; understanding how to instantiate and populate a Sequential model is distinct from the layers themselves.

candidates.label: Dense (fully connected) layer
candidates.description: Dense layers are fully connected layers where each neuron receives input from all neurons of the previous layer; defined with number of neurons and activation function.
coverage_criteria: Student can add a Dense layer in Keras specifying the number of nodes and activation argument.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Source explains 'Fully connected layers are defined using the Dense class.' and shows model.add(Dense(12, activation='relu')).
rationale.granularity_rationale: It is a fundamental building block of neural networks; understanding its parameters is essential for constructing models.

candidates.label: Input shape specification
candidates.description: The first layer of a neural network must receive the correct number of input features, specified via the input_shape argument (e.g., input_shape=(8,)).
coverage_criteria: Student can set input_shape correctly on the first Dense layer to match the number of features in the dataset.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly says 'ensure the input layer has the correct number of input features... specified with the input_shape argument and setting it to (8,)'.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific detail that can trip beginners; checking understanding of input dimensions is a focused question.

candidates.label: ReLU activation function
candidates.description: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation returns 0 for negative input and the input value for positive input; commonly used in hidden layers for better performance.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that ReLU helps avoid vanishing gradient and is preferred in hidden layers over sigmoid/tanh.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Source notes 'These days, better performance is achieved using the ReLU activation function' and uses it in the first two layers.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Activation functions are critical components; ReLU is a widely used choice and the source explicitly discusses its advantages and demonstrates its usage.

candidates.label: Overfitting and Underfitting
candidates.description: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data noise, resulting in poor generalization; underfitting occurs when the model is too simple to capture patterns. Techniques like regularization and dropout help prevent overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Define overfitting and underfitting with examples.
Suggest at least one technique to combat overfitting.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The 'MACHINE LEARNING IN EMOJI' section mentions 'Overfitting' and the Keras cheat sheet shows dropout layer usage, while the chart includes DRN which addresses the vanishing gradient problem.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a fundamental challenge in machine learning; the candidate covers the concepts and common remedies.

anchors: MACHINE LEARNING IN EMOJI: NEURAL NET prone to overfitting

candidates.label: Dropout Regularization
candidates.description: Dropout prevents overfitting by randomly dropping neurons with probability p during training, keeping them with probability 1-p.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain the purpose of dropout, describe how it works during training, and state the typical range for p.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source clearly defines dropout and explains its purpose of preventing overfitting.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a concise technique that can be checked by asking about its mechanism and purpose.

candidates.label: Linear Vector Spaces in Neural Networks
candidates.description: The mathematical foundation for neural network computations, defining vector spaces, inner products, norms, and linear transformations that underlie neuron operations and weight updates.
coverage_criteria: Define a linear vector space and list its axioms.
Compute the inner product of two given vectors.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source begins with a detailed definition of linear vector spaces, spanning, inner products, and norms, which are essential for understanding neural network mathematics.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This candidate covers the required linear algebra concepts at a level testable with simple computational checks.

candidates.label: Gradient Descent Optimization
candidates.description: An iterative algorithm for minimizing a function by repeatedly taking steps proportional to the negative gradient; variants like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Adam are widely used to train neural networks.
coverage_criteria: Explain the update rule of gradient descent.
Name one adaptive learning rate optimizer and its advantage.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source includes a 'General Minimization Algorithm', 'Steepest Descent Algorithm', and lists TensorFlow optimizers like Adam, Adagrad, etc., which are all based on gradient descent.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This candidate captures the core optimization principle; it is checkable by the basic algorithm and common variants.

candidates.label: Learning Rate and Adam Optimizer
candidates.description: The learning rate η determines the step size for weight updates. Adam is an adaptive learning rate method that adjusts η per parameter.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain the role of the learning rate in training and describe that Adam adapts the learning rate.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source describes the learning rate as controlling weight update pace and states that Adam is a popular adaptive method.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept combines the basic idea of learning rate with a notable optimizer, checkable with a short explanation question.

candidates.label: Gradient Descent
candidates.description: Gradient descent minimizes the cost function by updating each parameter by subtracting the product of the learning rate and the parameter's gradient.
coverage_criteria: Write the parameter update rule.
Explain the role of the learning rate.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The article explains that gradient descent uses gradients to update weights and biases to minimize cost, and the update_parameters function implements this.
rationale.granularity_rationale: A fundamental optimization step that can be checked with a simple update rule question.

candidates.label: Treinamento com Gradiente Descendente em Redes Neurais
candidates.description: O gradiente descendente é usado para ajustar os pesos de uma rede neural iterativamente, minimizando uma função de perda (como erro quadrático) ao longo de épocas sobre o conjunto de treinamento.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve explicar o papel do gradiente descendente no treinamento de redes neurais.
O estudante deve compreender o conceito de época e atualização de pesos.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O texto mostra o loop de treinamento com gradiente descendente para XOR e Fizz Buzz, calculando gradientes e atualizando a rede.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Implementação prática do treinamento; pode ser verificado com perguntas sobre o loop e o papel da taxa de aprendizado.

candidates.label: Taxa de Aprendizado
candidates.description: Hiperparâmetro que controla a magnitude da correção dos pesos a cada iteração; valores pequenos tornam o treinamento mais lento, valores grandes podem destabilizar.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve prever o efeito de aumentar ou diminuir a taxa de aprendizado no número de épocas necessárias para convergir.
O aluno deve identificar um valor inadequado (ex: 0 ou negativo) como causa de não-convergência.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo mostra ao vivo a alteração da taxa de aprendizado (de 0.01 para 0.001) e discute o impacto direto no número de épocas (28 para 112), fornecendo evidência clara da sua importância.
rationale.granularity_rationale: O conceito é compacto e observável através de experimentos simples com o código fornecido.

anchors: 51:50 Perceptron summary and impact of learning rate
40:05 Addressing a bug in w_fit and taxa_aprendiz

candidates.label: Época
candidates.description: Uma época representa uma passagem completa sobre todos os exemplos de treinamento; o número de épocas é usado como critério de parada no treinamento.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve distinguir iteração (sobre um exemplo) de época (sobre todo o dataset).
O aluno deve explicar por que limitar o número de épocas evita loops infinitos.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O código implementa um contador de épocas (`epoca += 1`) e o vídeo explica que a época serve como limite de convergência quando a rede não encontra separação perfeita (25:16-26:00).
rationale.granularity_rationale: A primeira abordagem de época é simples, mas suficiente para entender o funcionamento básico do loop de treino e pode ser verificada com perguntas de interpretação de código.

candidates.label: Bias (Viés)
candidates.description: Termo constante adicionado à combinação linear das entradas, representado pelo peso w0 associado a uma entrada fixa de -1, que permite deslocar a fronteira de decisão.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve identificar o papel do bias em permitir que a reta de separação não passe pela origem.
O aluno deve explicar como o bias é tratado no código (entrada -1 com peso w0) no cálculo do somatório.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo descreve o bias como um 'limiar de ativação' e mostra sua implementação no código (`w[0] * -1`) (06:01-06:27, 29:35-29:41).
rationale.granularity_rationale: O bias é um componente matemático bem definido que pode ser verificado isoladamente no contexto do modelo linear.

candidates.label: Forward Propagation
candidates.description: Forward propagation computes the output of a neural network by sequentially applying linear transformations (weights and biases) and activation functions from the input layer to the output layer.
coverage_criteria: Describe the steps of forward propagation for a simple network.
Explain why we store caches during forward propagation.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The article explains forward propagation as the process of generating an output from input, and provides a Python implementation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This core algorithmic step can be tested by asking to trace the computations in a small example.

candidates.label: Neural Network Parameter Initialization
candidates.description: Before training, weights should be initialized with small random values and biases can be initialized as zeros to break symmetry and enable effective gradient updates.
coverage_criteria: Explain why random initialization is needed for weights.
Describe the effect of initializing weights with zeros.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The init_params function initializes weights with random values and biases with zeros, highlighting the need for symmetry breaking.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Initialization is a critical step; the rationale can be checked with a couple of questions.

candidates.label: Neural Network Training Process
candidates.description: Training a neural network involves iterating over the dataset multiple times (epochs), each time performing forward propagation, cost computation, backpropagation, and parameter updates.
coverage_criteria: List the steps in one training iteration.
Explain what an epoch is.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The train function encapsulates the entire training loop, calling forward_prop, cost_function, backprop, and update_parameters for a number of epochs.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This high-level process is learnable and testable with a sequence of steps.

candidates.label: Layer Dimensions in Neural Networks
candidates.description: The layer_dims list specifies the number of neurons in each layer (input, hidden, output), and determines the shape of parameters (weights: (current layer, previous layer); biases: (current layer, 1)).
coverage_criteria: Given layer dimensions, determine the shape of W1.
Explain why biases are vectors of shape (n_l, 1).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The article uses layer_dims to initialize parameters and loop through layers, explaining the shapes.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Understanding parameter shapes is key for implementation and can be checked with a shape identification question.

candidates.label: Caching in Forward Propagation
candidates.description: To enable efficient backpropagation, forward propagation stores caches containing linear input (A_prev, W, b) and activation input (Z) for each layer.
coverage_criteria: Explain why caching is necessary for backpropagation.
Identify which values are cached for a given layer.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The forward_prop function explicitly stores linear and activation caches, and backprop uses them to compute gradients.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Caching is a practical detail for implementing backprop; testable with a reason and content question.

candidates.label: Perceptron e Função Degrau
candidates.description: O perceptron é a rede neural mais simples: um único neurônio que calcula uma soma ponderada das entradas e dispara se o resultado ≥ 0, usando a função degrau (step function).
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve ser capaz de explicar o funcionamento do perceptron, incluindo pesos, viés (bias) e função degrau.
O estudante deve implementar um perceptron para comportamentos lógicos simples como AND e OR.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O texto apresenta o perceptron como a rede mais simples, explica a função degrau e mostra exemplos de portas lógicas (AND, OR, NOT).
rationale.granularity_rationale: O perceptron é uma unidade fundamental, com tamanho adequado para ser verificado com questões diretas sobre seu cálculo e limitações.

candidates.label: Limitação do Perceptron e XOR
candidates.description: Um único perceptron não pode resolver problemas não linearmente separáveis, como a porta XOR, sendo necessárias redes com múltiplos neurônios.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve identificar que a porta XOR não pode ser implementada por um perceptron simples.
O estudante deve justificar a necessidade de redes com camadas ocultas para resolver XOR.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O texto afirma explicitamente que alguns problemas, como XOR, não podem ser resolvidos por um perceptron e motiva a transição para redes mais complexas.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Este conceito é específico e verificável: basta perguntar se XOR é possível com perceptron e por quê.

candidates.label: Linearmente Separável
candidates.description: Propriedade de um problema onde é possível traçar uma linha (ou hiperplano) que separa perfeitamente as classes; o perceptron simples só resolve problemas desse tipo.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve identificar se um conjunto de pontos 2D é linearmente separável visualizando o gráfico.
O aluno deve prever se um perceptron simples será capaz de classificar corretamente um dado dataset linearmente não-separável.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo menciona explicitamente que o perceptron 'só resolve problemas linearmente separáveis' (05:14) e demonstra o impacto usando um dataset não-linear, tornando a ideia central para a compreensão das limitações.
rationale.granularity_rationale: A noção é bem delimitada e pode ser avaliada com exercícios de classificação de distribuições 2D simples.

anchors: 52:57 Conclusão e experimentação com não-linearmente separável

candidates.label: Algoritmo de Treinamento do Perceptron
candidates.description: Processo iterativo que ajusta os pesos do perceptron com base no erro entre a saída predita e a desejada, usando a regra: w = w + taxa_aprendiz * (d - y) * x.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve ser capaz de escrever o pseudocódigo do treinamento do perceptron (cálculo de u, ativação, comparação e atualização de pesos).
O aluno deve explicar o papel da correção do erro na convergência da rede.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: A maior parte do vídeo é dedicada à implementação passo a passo do algoritmo de treinamento (código e explicação das funções `perceptron_fit`, `ajuste`, `sinal`), evidenciando que é um conceito essencial.
rationale.granularity_rationale: O escopo cobre apenas o loop principal de treino e a regra de atualização, formando uma unidade de conhecimento verificável com perguntas de implementação.

candidates.label: Codificação de Entradas para Redes Neurais
candidates.description: Para alimentar redes neurais com dados não vetoriais, é necessário codificá-los em vetores. Exemplos incluem codificação binária de números inteiros e one-hot encoding para classes de saída.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve propor uma representação vetorial adequada para um problema simples (ex.: números ou categorias).
O estudante deve explicar a codificação binária e one-hot encoding como estratégias.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: No exemplo Fizz Buzz, o texto discute como transformar números em representações binárias e classes em vetores one-hot.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Habilidade prática de engenharia de features; pode ser verificada pedindo para codificar um pequeno conjunto de dados.

candidates.label: Dataset para Redes Neurais
candidates.description: Conjunto de dados estruturados com atributos (features) e classes alvo; para o perceptron é necessário que os dados sejam numéricos e idealmente linearmente separáveis.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve examinar um arquivo CSV e identificar as colunas de atributos e a coluna alvo.
O aluno deve sugerir transformações de dados categóricos para numéricos para uso em redes neurais.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo carrega um dataset CSV, explica sua estrutura (atributos vs alvo) e discute como buscar datasets no Kaggle/UCI e a necessidade de conversão de dados (09:44-10:00, 19:50-20:50, 57:47-59:30).
rationale.granularity_rationale: O tópico pode ser avaliado pedindo ao aluno para preparar um pequeno dataset para treinamento do perceptron.

candidates.label: Resolução de XOR com Rede Multicamadas
candidates.description: O problema XOR pode ser resolvido por uma rede feed-forward com uma camada oculta que calcula características (AND e OR) e uma camada de saída que combina essas características.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve descrever como uma rede de duas camadas pode implementar XOR.
O estudante deve identificar o papel da camada oculta em extrair features como AND e OR.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O texto apresenta uma rede manual para XOR, explicando como a camada oculta computa AND e OR e a saída combina para XOR.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Exemplo concreto de aplicação de rede feed-forward para problema não linear; verificável pedindo explicação da arquitetura.

candidates.label: Exemplo de Aplicação: Fizz Buzz com Rede Neural
candidates.description: O problema Fizz Buzz pode ser resolvido treinando uma rede neural com entrada codificada binariamente e saída one-hot, demonstrando capacidade de aprendizado de padrões númericos.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve explicar a transformação do problema Fizz Buzz para um problema de classificação usando redes neurais.
O estudante deve descrever a arquitetura usada: 10 entradas, 25 neurônios ocultos, 4 saídas.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O capítulo inteiro usa Fizz Buzz como exemplo prático de aplicação de redes neurais, desde codificação até treinamento e avaliação.
rationale.granularity_rationale: End-to-end example que consolida vários conceitos; pode ser verificado com perguntas sobre as escolhas de codificação e arquitetura.
